title: Navigable small worlds
description: Small-world graphs have short paths between any two nodes via a mix of local and long-range links — Milgram's six degrees, engineered. Kleinberg showed greedy routing works when long links follow the right distribution; HNSW turned it into the best ANN index. The property that matters: from any node, greedy steps toward the target make progress, so search is O(log n) hops.
mechanism: Local links for clustering + long-range links with distance-decaying probability. Greedy routing: move to the neighbor closest to the target; repeat. Works when the link distribution matches the space.
algo: O(log n) greedy hops with the right link distribution; O(n) without it.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(1)
N = 200
# ring lattice + long-range links with distance-decaying probability (Kleinberg)
g = {i: {(i-1) % N, (i+1) % N} for i in range(N)}
for i in range(N):
    for _ in range(2):
        d = int(random.paretovariate(1.5)) % N
        g[i].add((i + d) % N)

def greedy(s, t):
    cur, hops, seen = s, 0, set()
    while cur != t and cur not in seen:
        seen.add(cur)
        cur = min(g[cur], key=lambda n: min(abs(n-t), N-abs(n-t)))
        hops += 1
    return hops, cur == t

hops = [greedy(0, N//2)[0] for _ in range(20)]
print('greedy hops 0->%d: avg %.1f (log-scale, not N=%d)' % (N//2, sum(hops)/len(hops), N))

title: HNSW layers
description: HNSW's layers are the hierarchy: layer 0 holds every vector with dense local links; higher layers hold exponentially fewer vectors with longer links. Search starts at the top (coarse, fast) and descends, refining at each layer. The layer assignment (random, exponential) is what makes the structure a hierarchy rather than a flat graph — and hierarchy is what makes search logarithmic.
mechanism: Level ~ floor(-ln(uniform) * mL); insert top-down, connecting M neighbors per layer. Search: greedy per layer from the top, beam search (ef) at layer 0.
algo: Expected max layer O(log n); search O(log n) layers x local beam.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(2)
N, ML = 10000, 0.3
levels = [int(-math.log(random.random()) * ML) for _ in range(N)]
from collections import Counter
c = Counter(levels)
print('level : vectors (exponential decay)')
for l in sorted(c):
    print('%5d : %5d %s' % (l, c[l], '#' * min(40, c[l] // 20)))
print('top layer: a handful of long-range hubs; bottom: everyone, dense local')

title: Beam search on graphs
description: Beam search generalizes greedy: keep the ef best candidates seen, expand the closest unvisited, and stop when no unexpanded candidate can beat the worst in the beam. ef=1 is greedy; larger ef explores more and recalls more. It is the query algorithm for HNSW and DiskANN — the ef knob is the recall-latency dial, and the search is interruptible (deadline = return the beam).
mechanism: Priority queue of candidates by distance; visited set; expand closest; maintain top-ef results. Terminate when the closest unexpanded candidate is worse than the ef-th result.
algo: O(ef * degree) expansions typical; larger ef = more recall, more work.

title: Graph construction
description: Building the graph is the expensive part: naive O(n^2) neighbor search does not scale, so construction uses the same search it will serve — insert vectors one by one, searching the partial graph for neighbors (NN-descent refines iteratively). Parameters (M, efConstruction) trade build time for graph quality; a better graph means faster queries forever, so construction quality pays off over the index lifetime.
mechanism: Incremental: for each vector, beam-search the existing graph for candidates, link the best M (with diversity pruning). NN-descent: start random, iteratively improve neighborhoods. Prune for diversity (HNSW heuristic).
algo: O(n log n) incremental; quality from efConstruction and pruning.
demo:
import random, math, heapq
random.seed(4)
N, D, M = 200, 6, 6
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x-y)**2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

g = {}
for i, v in enumerate(vecs):  # incremental: search the partial graph
    if i == 0:
        g[i] = []
        continue
    cands = heapq.nsmallest(20, ((dist(v, vecs[j]), j) for j in range(i)))
    g[i] = [j for _, j in cands[:M]]
    for _, j in cands[:M]:  # back-links
        g[j] = (g.get(j, []) + [i])[:M*2]

avg_deg = sum(len(v) for v in g.values()) / N
print('built graph: %d nodes, avg degree %.1f' % (N, avg_deg))
print('each insert searched the partial graph: O(n log n), quality compounds')

title: Degree pruning and diversity
description: Naive k-nearest links cluster in one direction — the graph needs diverse directions to route well. HNSW's pruning heuristic keeps a neighbor only if it is closer to the node than to any already-kept neighbor, spreading links across directions. Diversity beats raw proximity for navigability: a graph that can go every direction routes greedily; a clustered one gets stuck.
mechanism: Candidate neighbors sorted by distance; keep candidate c if dist(node, c) < min over kept k of dist(k, c) (or with slack). Caps degree at M while maximizing directional coverage.
algo: O(candidates^2) per node at build; query-time payoff in fewer hops.
demo:
import math
# node at origin; candidates mostly east, one north. Keep diverse directions.
cands = [(10, 0), (11, 1), (9, -1), (0, 10), (10.5, 0.5)]

def d(a, b):
    return math.dist(a, b)

kept = []
for c in sorted(cands, key=lambda p: d((0, 0), p)):
    if all(d((0, 0), c) < d(k, c) for k in kept):  # closer to node than to any kept
        kept.append(c)
print('candidates:', cands)
print('kept:', kept, '(east cluster represented once; north kept: directions covered)')
print('diversity > proximity for navigability')

title: Graph embeddings
description: Graph embeddings turn nodes into vectors preserving structure: neighbors embed nearby (DeepWalk random walks, node2vec biased walks), so the graph becomes searchable by vector similarity. The pipeline is walk -> corpus -> word2vec; the result powers recommendations ('users like this also...') and feeds the ANN indexes in this lane. Structure becomes geometry.
mechanism: Random walks generate node sequences; skip-gram learns embeddings; cosine similarity finds related nodes. node2vec biases walks (BFS vs DFS) toward community or structural similarity.
algo: O(walks * length) corpus; word2vec O(corpus). Inference O(1) per node after.

title: Graph traversal algorithms
description: BFS and DFS are the graph's legs: BFS explores by distance (shortest paths, level by level), DFS goes deep (topological sort, cycle detection). On indexed graphs they run over adjacency with visited sets; on billion-node graphs they become distributed (Pregel-style message passing). Every graph query — reachability, shortest path, components — composes these two.
mechanism: BFS: queue, O(V+E). DFS: stack/recursion, O(V+E). Distributed: vertex-centric supersteps. Bidirectional BFS halves the explored space for point-to-point queries.
algo: O(V+E) single-machine; bidirectional O(b^(d/2)) for branching b, depth d.

title: Community detection
description: Communities are dense subgraphs — friend groups, topic clusters, fraud rings. Louvain greedily maximizes modularity (dense inside, sparse between) by moving nodes between communities; label propagation spreads the majority label. Detection runs on the index's own graph to find structure worth exposing: 'people who bought X also form a community around Y'.
mechanism: Louvain: iterative local moves maximizing modularity gain, then aggregate. Label propagation: adopt the most common neighbor label, repeat. Both near-linear in practice.
algo: O(E) per pass typical; converges in few passes.

title: Shortest path indexing
description: Point-to-point shortest paths on huge graphs need indexes: landmarks (distances to a few hub nodes bound any query via triangle inequality), contraction hierarchies (preprocess node order, query bidirectional over the hierarchy), and hub labeling (each node stores distances to its hubs; query intersects labels). Road networks use contraction hierarchies for millisecond routes; social graphs use landmarks.
mechanism: Landmarks: dist(s,t) >= |dist(s,L) - dist(t,L)| for pruning/A*. Contraction hierarchies: contract least-important nodes first, add shortcuts. Hub labeling: precompute, query by label intersection.
algo: Query milliseconds on continental road networks after O(E log V)-ish preprocessing.
demo:
import heapq
# landmark lower bound: |dist(s,L) - dist(t,L)| <= dist(s,t) (triangle inequality)
g = {'a': [('b', 2), ('c', 5)], 'b': [('a', 2), ('d', 3)], 'c': [('a', 5), ('d', 1)], 'd': [('b', 3), ('c', 1)]}

def dij(s):
    dist, pq = {s: 0}, [(0, s)]
    while pq:
        d, n = heapq.heappop(pq)
        for m, w in g[n]:
            if d + w < dist.get(m, 1e9):
                dist[m] = d + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (d + w, m))
    return dist

L = 'a'
dL = dij(L)
s, t = 'b', 'c'
print('dist from landmark a:', dL)
print('lower bound dist(b,c) >= |%d - %d| = %d' % (dL['b'], dL['c'], abs(dL['b'] - dL['c'])))
print('true dist(b,c) =', dij('b')['c'], '(bound prunes A* search)')

title: Knowledge graphs as indexes
description: Knowledge graphs index the world's facts as triples, and the graph structure is the query engine: multi-hop questions become traversals, entity resolution becomes node merging, and inference (transitive IS-A) is precomputed. title: Incremental graph updates
description: Graphs change — new vectors, new edges — and rebuilding HNSW from scratch is too slow. Incremental insertion searches the existing graph for neighbors and splices the node in (HNSW is natively incremental); deletions mark tombstones and lazily repair (or rebuild in the background). The hard part is quality decay: the graph degrades over many updates, so production systems rebuild periodically off the update log.
mechanism: Insert: beam search + link (same as construction). Delete: tombstone + neighbor repair, or periodic rebuild. Track quality metrics (recall on a probe set); rebuild when it dips.
algo: Insert O(log n); delete O(degree) lazy. Rebuild amortized over updates.

title: Memory layout for graphs
description: Graph search is pointer-chasing — cache misses dominate. Layout optimizations: adjacency arrays (not linked lists), node data interleaved with hot fields first, communities clustered on pages (reorder by BFS for locality), and quantized vectors inline. The difference between naive and tuned layout is 2-5x query throughput on the same graph. Profile cache misses, not just time.
mechanism: CSR (compressed sparse row) adjacency; reorder nodes by community/BFS; separate hot/cold fields; align to cache lines. Measure with perf (cache-miss rate).
algo: O(E) reorder once; queries 2-5x faster from locality.
demo:
# BFS reorder: neighbors become adjacent in memory -> fewer cache misses
from collections import deque

g = {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 3], 2: [0, 3], 3: [1, 2, 4], 4: [3]}
order, seen, q = [], {0}, deque([0])
while q:
    n = q.popleft()
    order.append(n)
    for m in g[n]:
        if m not in seen:
            seen.add(m)
            q.append(m)
print('BFS order:', order, '(neighbors adjacent in the array)')
print('CSR adjacency + this order: the query walk stays in cache lines')
print('2-5x throughput from layout alone on the same graph')

title: Billion-scale graph systems
description: Billion-node graphs do not fit one machine: they shard by node (edge-cut or vertex-cut), replicate hot nodes, and run queries as distributed traversals (Pregel supersteps) or sharded ANN (each shard searches locally, merge). The engineering is in the cut — vertex-cut (PowerGraph) handles power-law graphs where edge-cut fails — and in keeping the per-shard work balanced.
mechanism: Partition (hash or METIS); vertex-cut for power-law; distributed beam search with per-shard top-k merged globally. Hot-node replication cuts cross-shard traffic.
algo: O(shards) fan-out per query; merge O(shards * k). Cut quality decides the network cost.
demo:
# vertex-cut: high-degree nodes split across shards (power-law graphs)
import hashlib
SHARDS = 4
# edge-cut would put hub node 0's 1M edges on ONE shard (hotspot)
# vertex-cut: edges of hub hashed across shards
edges = [(0, i) for i in range(8)]  # hub 0

def shard_edge(a, b):
    return int(hashlib.md5(('%d-%d' % (a, b)).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % SHARDS

placement = {}
for a, b in edges:
    placement.setdefault(shard_edge(a, b), []).append((a, b))
print('hub edges across shards:', {s: len(e) for s, e in placement.items()})
print('vertex-cut: no single shard holds the hub (edge-cut would hotspot)')

title: Graph indexes in production
description: Production graph indexes need what papers skip: monitoring (recall probes, latency histograms), safe updates (blue-green index swaps), capacity planning (RAM per vector x vectors), and incident playbooks (recall dropped — check efSearch, then data drift, then the graph). The index is a service with SLOs, not a data structure — operate it like one.
mechanism: Recall probe set run continuously; blue-green deploys for rebuilds; autoscale on latency; runbooks per symptom. Version the index with the code that built it.
algo: O(probe set) monitoring; the ops are organizational.
